note: Refreshed every week by the program's research task. Each item says what changed, why it matters to a data engineer or architect, and how to test the claim yourself.

items.title: Snowflake: dynamic tables with REFRESH_MODE = AUTO now resolve to ADAPTIVE, not INCREMENTAL
items.summary: From 20 November 2026, a new dynamic table left on the default AUTO refresh mode resolves to ADAPTIVE when its query supports it, and to FULL otherwise. Tables that already exist keep the mode they resolved to. Setting REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL explicitly keeps the old behaviour.
items.why: A changed default changes your bill and your freshness without anyone touching the code. An architect pins the refresh mode of every production dynamic table in code review, the same way you pin a library version, and reads the resolved mode after each deploy.
items.try: In module 8's build step, write the dynamic table twice, once with the default and once with REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL, and note which one you would let reach production and why.

items.title: Snowflake: COPY INTO and Snowpipe log bad rows and enforce CHECK constraints (generally available)
items.summary: Generally available on 19 November 2026. Tables with error logging or CHECK constraints now reject rows that break them during COPY INTO and Snowpipe loads and write those rows to an error table; loads into other tables behave as before.
items.why: This is the dead-letter pattern moved into the warehouse load itself: good rows land, bad rows are kept with the reason, and nothing is silently dropped. It also means a constraint added for safety can start rejecting rows a pipeline used to accept, so add one with an alert on the error table.
items.try: In module 9, sketch how you would split a batch into accepted and rejected rows with the reason for each, then count how many rejects would page someone.

items.title: dbt v2 engine is generally available, with batch testing
items.summary: dbt's November update (17 November 2026) makes the v2 engine generally available on Redshift, Databricks, BigQuery, Snowflake and DuckDB, with ClickHouse and Spark in beta. Batch testing, opt-in with --batch-tests, runs a model's unique and not_null tests as one query per test type; local unit tests in DuckDB are in alpha.
items.why: Test cost is a real line on a warehouse bill: hundreds of small test queries each scan the table. Batching them is the same trade-off as batching any small request, and an interviewer may ask how you would cut the cost of dbt tests without dropping coverage.
items.try: In module 4's dbt build, count the test queries one dbt test run sends for a model with four tested columns, then count them again as if unique and not_null were batched.

items.title: Databricks: add and backfill Delta columns without rewriting the unchanged columns (beta)
items.summary: In beta from 13 November 2026, enabled by an admin on the Previews page. Adding and backfilling a column on a Delta table writes only the new column's data instead of rewriting every data file.
items.why: On copy-on-write tables a backfill of one column has always meant rewriting the whole table. Writing only the changed column turns a multi-terabyte rewrite into a small write, which changes how you plan schema changes and backfills.
items.try: In module 8's DeltaTable lab, add a column and backfill it, then count the add and remove commits in _delta_log and compare with what a column-only write would need.

items.title: Databricks: system table retention from 30 days to 10 years (generally available)
items.summary: Generally available on 18 November 2026. Retention for system tables is set account-wide from 30 to 3,650 days; the first 395 days are free and longer retention adds storage charges.
items.why: System tables hold the usage, billing and audit history that showback and audits run on. Choosing their retention is a platform-as-a-product decision: long enough for a year-over-year cost review and an audit, short enough not to pay for history nobody reads.
items.try: In module O4, write the retention you would set and the two questions it must answer (last year's cost per team, and who read a table eleven months ago).

items.title: Confluent Cloud: back up and restore whole Kafka records through Azure Blob Storage
items.summary: Added on 18 November 2026. The Azure Blob Storage sink and source connectors can save and restore full records, with keys, values, headers and metadata, using the BACKUP_FULL_RECORD and RESTORE_BACKUP_FULL_RECORD modes.
items.why: Retention is not a backup: once a segment ages out, the data is gone. Keeping keys and headers matters, because a restore without keys loses partitioning and ordering, and one without headers loses tracing and schema ids.
items.try: In module 5, list what a restored topic must keep to be usable (key, partition order, headers, schema id) and which of those a plain value-only export would lose.
